title_en: Maersk (China) Shipping Co., Ltd. and Its Xiamen Branch v. Xiamen Yinghai Industrial Development Co., Ltd. and China Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency Co., Ltd. — dispute over compensation for damage to international maritime freight forwarding operation rights (retrial)
ruling_gist_en: Public transport performs the social function of providing transport services to the public, and is characterized by public welfare and monopoly. In order to protect the public interest, Article 289 of the Contract Law of the PRC provides: 'A carrier engaged in public transport shall not refuse normal and reasonable transport requests from passengers or consignors.' International container liner shipping is a commercial business activity serving international trade. It does not belong to public utilities, does not have public welfare nature, nor is it monopolistic, and therefore does not constitute public transport. A consignor or its freight forwarder that requests a carrier engaged in international container liner shipping to assume a compulsory contracting obligation has no legal basis, and such request should be dismissed.
keywords_en: civil; dispute over compensation for damage to right to operate as a maritime freight forwarding agent; retrial; Supreme People's Court; Beijing; Fujian Province; legal person; Contract Law; whether international container liner shipping constitutes public transport; whether the carrier has a compulsory contracting obligation; reversal of judgment; container transport cooperation; refusal to provide containers; dispute over seal fees; clarifying that international container liner shipping does not belong to public transport; denying the carrier's compulsory contracting obligation; maritime freight forwarding agency right damage compensation dispute
full_text_en:
Maersk (China) Shipping Co., Ltd. and Its Xiamen Branch v. Xiamen Yinghai Industrial Development Co., Ltd. and China Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency Co., Ltd. — Retrial Case Concerning Dispute over Damages for Right to Operate International Maritime Freight Forwarding Agency

【Ruling Summary】

A public carrier performs the social function of providing transport services to the general public and is characterized by public welfare and monopoly. To safeguard the public interest, Article 289 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "A carrier engaging in public transport shall not reject the normal, reasonable transportation requests of passengers or consignors." International maritime container liner shipping is a commercial business activity serving international trade; it does not belong to a public utility, lacks the nature of public welfare, and is not monopolistic. Therefore, it does not constitute public transport. A consignor or its freight forwarder has no legal basis to request that a carrier engaged in international maritime container liner shipping assume a compulsory contracting obligation, and such a request shall be dismissed.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2010) Min Ti Zi No. 213

Retrial Applicant (Defendant at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Maersk (China) Shipping Co., Ltd. Domicile: 17/F, Tower B, Lotte Center, No. 24, East Third Ring Middle Road, Chaoyang District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Andreas Oskar Hoch, Chairman of the Board of the Company.

Authorized Agent: Yang Wengui, Attorney at Beijing Haitong Law Firm.

Authorized Agent: Peng Xianwei, Attorney at Beijing Haitong Law Firm.

Retrial Applicant (Defendant at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Maersk (China) Shipping Co., Ltd., Xiamen Branch. Domicile: 19/F, International Bank Building, No. 8, Lujiang Road, Siming District, Xiamen City, Fujian Province.

Person in Charge: Xu Lixin, General Manager of the Branch.

Authorized Agent: Yang Wengui, Attorney at Beijing Haitong Law Firm.

Authorized Agent: Peng Xianwei, Attorney at Beijing Haitong Law Firm.

Retrial Respondent (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Xiamen Yinghai Industrial Development Co., Ltd. Domicile: Room 1112, Luhui Building, No. 65, Haitian Road, Huli District, Xiamen City, Fujian Province.

Legal Representative: Cai Yuanyou, Chairman and General Manager of the Company.

Authorized Agent: Wang Muxin, Attorney at Beijing Haolimo Law Firm.

Third Party at First Instance: China Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency Co., Ltd. Domicile: 15/F, Shipping Building, No. 809, Songyu Middle Road, Haicang District, Xiamen City, Fujian Province.

Legal Representative: Ke Dong, Chairman of the Board of the Company.

Authorized Agent: Gao Honghong, Employee of China Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency Co., Ltd.

In the case concerning the dispute over damages for the right to operate international maritime freight forwarding agency between the retrial applicants Maersk (China) Shipping Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Maersk Company) and Maersk (China) Shipping Co., Ltd., Xiamen Branch (hereinafter referred to as Xiamen Branch) and the retrial respondent Xiamen Yinghai Industrial Development Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Yinghai Company), and the third party at first instance China Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency), the Fujian High People's Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of second instance) rendered a civil judgment (2008) Min Min Zhong Zi No. 381 on October 22, 2008, which has become legally effective. Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch, dissatisfied with the judgment, applied to this Court for retrial. This Court, by a civil ruling (2010) Min Shen Zi No. 1552 on December 7, 2010, decided to bring the case up for retrial. In accordance with the law, this Court formed a collegial panel with Adjudicator Liu Shoujie as the presiding judge, and Acting Adjudicators Guo Zhonghong and Yu Xiaohan participating in the deliberation, and held a public hearing on March 24, 2011. The authorized agents of the retrial applicants Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch, Yang Wengui and Peng Xianwei, and the legal representative of the retrial respondent Yinghai Company, Cai Yuanyou, together with its authorized agent Wang Muxin, appeared in court to participate in the proceedings. The third party at first instance, Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency, was duly served with summons by this Court but did not appear, submitting only a written response. The case has now been concluded.

The following facts were found at first instance by the Xiamen Maritime Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance): On October 31, 2003, Yinghai Company and Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency signed the "Container Transport Cooperation Agreement," stipulating that: Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency, acting as a container agent, was authorized by the maritime carrier or container operator, based on the procedures submitted by Yinghai Company, to deliver containers under its agency to Yinghai Company, which would undertake the land transport business, including the haulage of import and export containers; for the haulage of import containers, Yinghai Company would apply to Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency for container release, and upon approval, would pick up loaded containers from the terminal designated by Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency, deliver them to the consignee, and then return empty containers; for the haulage of export containers, Yinghai Company would apply to Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency for container release, obtain an equipment interchange receipt for export empty containers issued by Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency, pick up empty containers at the terminal or place designated by Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency, then deliver them to the shipper; after the shipper completed loading, Yinghai Company would transport the loaded containers to the terminal designated by Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency. In the same agreement, Yinghai Company and Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency also agreed on matters such as container use, maintenance, and detention charges, and also stipulated that the agreement would take effect from October 31, 2003, and terminate on December 31, 2003, and would be automatically renewed for one year if neither party objected upon expiration.

On March 15, 2005, Yinghai Company and Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency signed a new "Container Transport Cooperation Agreement," which adjusted the original agreement, stipulating that: Yinghai Company would apply to Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency for container release; upon verification without error, Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency would issue equipment interchange receipts for import loaded containers or export empty containers, except where Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency, as agent of the container owner or lessee, received clear instructions from the container owner or lessee not to deliver the equipment to Yinghai Company for use.

Prior to March 3, 2005, Yinghai Company was able to normally obtain Maersk Company's containers from Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency. On March 3, 2005, Maersk Company notified its agent Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency to cease providing Maersk Company's containers and container seals to Yinghai Company. Thereafter, Yinghai Company was unable to conduct any business related to the land transport of Maersk Company's containers.

Maersk Company primarily operated international container liner shipping at the Xiamen port and published sailing schedules through media such as "China Shipping Gazette." Effective August 1, 2004, Maersk Company increased the container seal fee at the Xiamen port to 45 yuan per container. The Xiamen Container Transport Association, Xiamen International Freight Forwarding Association, and Xiamen Foreign Economy and Trade Association elected 10 persons to form the "Xiamen Port Working Group for Requesting Shipping Companies to Cancel the Seal Fee." Cai Yuanyou, the legal representative of Yinghai Company, was elected as the group convener and one of the negotiation representatives, and negotiated with Maersk Company regarding the seal fee. Effective May 1, 2005, Maersk Company ceased collecting the seal fee at the Xiamen port, but Maersk Company stated that it had not canceled the seal fee but rather consolidated several fees including the seal fee into a single charge.

On November 10, 2005, Yinghai Company filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance on the grounds that Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch refused to accept its booking and consignment on behalf of cargo owners, causing losses. Its claims were: 1. Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch should immediately cease interfering with Yinghai Company's right to independent operation, remove the obstruction to the performance of the "Container Transport Cooperation Agreement" between Yinghai Company and Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency, and order Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch to provide cargo booking and related services to Yinghai Company and its principals in accordance with their business practices, and not refuse Yinghai Company's acceptance of commissions to handle container import and export freight and land container transport business related to Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch; 2. Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch should offer an apology to Yinghai Company, the content of which must be approved by Yinghai Company and published in media such as "Xiamen Daily," to eliminate the adverse impact on Yinghai Company; 3. Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch should jointly compensate Yinghai Company for economic losses of RMB 100; 4. Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch should jointly bear the notarized evidence preservation costs of RMB 1,535 incurred by Yinghai Company in investigating and gathering evidence.

The court of first instance held: March 3, 2005, was a gap period between the old and new "Container Transport Cooperation Agreements." Although Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch's notice to Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency not to release containers to Yinghai Company was the reason why Yinghai Company could not obtain containers, at that time, Yinghai Company lacked a contractual basis for container release. From March 15, 2005, the new "Container Transport Cooperation Agreement" between Yinghai Company and Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency came into effect. This agreement stipulated that when the container owner or lessee expressly indicated that the equipment should not be delivered to Yinghai Company for use, Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency had the right not to deliver the containers. Therefore, Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency's failure to deliver Maersk Company's containers had a contractual basis. A common carrier must be a transport enterprise with the nature of a public utility and public welfare. International liner shipping is a profit-making business, which does not fall within the scope of public utilities and does not have the character of public welfare. An international liner company is not a common carrier as defined in Article 289 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China. The provisions of that law regarding the compulsory contracting obligation of common carriers are not applicable to this case. Maersk Company's and Xiamen Branch's refusal to deal does not violate Chinese law. Yinghai Company filed the lawsuit on the ground of tort, but it could not prove the illegality of the actions of Maersk Company or Xiamen Branch; its claims could not be established. Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency was the agent of Maersk Company; the consequences of its actions within the scope of its agency should be borne by Maersk Company, and Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency did not bear tort liability. In summary, in accordance with Article 64, paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court of first instance rendered a civil judgment (2005) Xia Hai Fa Shi Chu Zi No. 48: dismissed all claims of Yinghai Company; the first-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 75 was to be borne by Yinghai Company.

Yinghai Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the court of second instance, arguing: 1. The sailing schedule offer publicly issued by Maersk Company to the society was not directed at a specific person; when Yinghai Company accepted the offer, Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch refused without legal basis. Yinghai Company's acceptance of Maersk Company's sailing schedule offer resulted in the formation and effectiveness of a transport contract. Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch's refusal to perform the transport contract constituted a breach of contract. 2. A common carrier should possess characteristics such as being open to the entire society, monopolistic, having freight rates subject to supervision by competent state authorities, and requiring special approval by competent state authorities for legal personality. Maersk Company fully possessed the above characteristics and was a common carrier, and should bear the compulsory contracting obligation according to law. 3. China is a contracting party to the United Nations Convention on a Code of Conduct for Liner Conferences. Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch's refusal to deal with Yinghai Company violated the basic principle of the Convention that there shall be no discrimination against shipowners or cargo owners of any country. 4. Yinghai Company has the right to engage in all legally permitted business activities within China, including transactions with Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch. The refusal to deal by Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch constituted a concurrence of tort and breach of contract, infringing upon Yinghai Company's lawful property rights and business rights. In summary, it requested the reversal of the first-instance judgment and support for its claims.

Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed, arguing: 1. Yinghai Company was an illegally established enterprise and had not obtained the qualification for international freight forwarding agency; thus it did not enjoy a lawful right to operate an international freight forwarding agency and accordingly did not have the corresponding right to claim. 2. During the first instance, Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch had fully adduced evidence proving Yinghai Company's dishonest conduct, which the court of first instance failed to adopt, resulting in unclear fact-finding. They requested the court of second instance to make findings and rulings on this issue.

In response to Yinghai Company's appeal, Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch submitted in their defense: 1. The requests and reasons in Yinghai Company's appeal had substantially changed its claims and reasons in the first instance. Yinghai Company claimed that the actions of Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch constituted a concurrence of breach of contract and tort; it should file a new lawsuit; otherwise, its modification of claims in the second instance should be dismissed. 2. Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch did not commit any breach of contract. Whether the sailing schedule was an offer or an invitation to offer, it had no relationship with Yinghai Company, which was a freight forwarder. A liner company is not a common carrier as defined in Article 289 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China; Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch should not bear a compulsory contracting obligation. The objective of the United Nations Convention on a Code of Conduct for Liner Conferences is to regulate the conduct of liner conferences; Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch are not bound by that Convention. The refusal to deal by Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch did not violate Chinese law and did not infringe upon Yinghai Company's property rights or business rights. Yinghai Company's claim that the actions of Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch constituted a concurrence of breach of contract and tort had no factual or legal basis. They therefore requested the dismissal of the appeal and affirmance of the original judgment.

In response to the appeal of Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch, Yinghai Company argued: Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch had no specific appellate requests. Their appeal should be dismissed.

The third party at first instance, Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency, submitted: As the agent of Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch, Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency acted in accordance with their instructions and should not bear any liability. Both Yinghai Company and Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch had no objection to this. It requested the court of second instance to uphold the first-instance judgment that Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency bore no liability.

After trial, the court of second instance confirmed that the facts found by the court of first instance were basically true and adopted them.

The court of second instance held: This case was a dispute over compensation for damages to the right to operate an international maritime freight forwarding agency. Yinghai Company's assertion in the second instance that the actions of Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch constituted a concurrence of breach of contract and tort was still aimed at the claim that Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch had infringed upon its business autonomy; it did not substantially change its claims in the first instance. Maersk Company's maritime transport operations, in addition to being commercial, also had a public welfare nature because they were open to the general public. Therefore, Maersk Company was a common carrier. Pursuant to Article 289 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, a common carrier bears a compulsory contracting obligation and shall not reject the normal, reasonable transportation requests of passengers or consignors. The sailing schedule notice issued by Maersk Company to the public was an invitation to offer. As long as a member of the public expressed an intention to contract (an offer) with Maersk Company, Maersk Company should not reject it without justifiable reason. Maersk Company's clear indication that it would not engage in business relations with Yinghai Company violated the compulsory contracting obligation of a common carrier and also violated Article 27 of the Regulations of the People's Republic of China on International Maritime Transportation, which provides that a liner company shall not abuse its dominant position by imposing restrictive conditions that cause harm to the counterparty in transactions. The United Nations Convention on a Code of Conduct for Liner Conferences, to which China has acceded, contains a principle that the various methods of liner conferences shall not discriminate against the shipowners, consignors, or foreign trade of any country. Maersk Company, as an international liner company registered in China, should also be bound by that Convention. The refusal to deal by Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch hindered the exercise of Yinghai Company's business autonomy; thus it should be ordered that Maersk Company shall not reject Yinghai Company's normal, reasonable transportation requests. Although the "Container Transport Cooperation Agreement" stipulated that when the container owner or lessee expressly indicated that the equipment should not be delivered to Yinghai Company for use, Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency had the right not to deliver the containers, this provision violated Article 289 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 27 of the Regulations of the People's Republic of China on International Maritime Transportation and should be held invalid. Maersk Company could not use this as a reason to refuse Yinghai Company's handling of container import and export freight and land container transport business related to Maersk Company. Yinghai Company was a lawfully established enterprise legal person. The reason Maersk Company did not engage in business dealings with Yinghai Company was not due to qualification issues, and Maersk Company also failed to adduce evidence proving that Yinghai Company had engaged in dishonest conduct. Therefore, the appellate arguments of Maersk Company were not adopted. Although Yinghai Company was denied the ability to obtain Maersk Company's containers and could not book space with Maersk Company, Yinghai Company could still book space with other shipping companies to achieve its transportation purpose. It failed to adduce evidence proving that it had suffered economic losses due to its inability to obtain Maersk Company's containers for land transport. Therefore, its claim for RMB 100 in economic losses was not supported. Maersk Company never denied that it had instructed Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency not to deal with Yinghai Company. The evidence preservation conducted by Yinghai Company to prove this fact had no practical significance; the resulting costs of RMB 1,535 should be borne by Yinghai Company itself. Yinghai Company's request for Maersk Company to publish an apology in the newspaper constituted compensation for mental damages; Yinghai Company had no such losses, so the request was not supported.

In summary, in accordance with Article 289 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 27 of the Regulations of the People's Republic of China on International Maritime Transportation, Article 64, paragraph 1 and Article 153, paragraph 1, subparagraph (2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court of second instance rendered the following judgment: 1. Set aside the civil judgment (2005) Xia Hai Fa Shi Chu Zi No. 48 of the Xiamen Maritime Court; 2. Order Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch not to refuse Yinghai Company's normal requests for booking and related transport services in accordance with business practices, not to refuse Yinghai Company's handling of container import and export freight and land container transport business related to Maersk Company, and to remove their obstruction to Yinghai Company's performance of the "Container Transport Cooperation Agreement" with Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency; 3. Dismiss all other claims of Yinghai Company; 4. Dismiss the appeals of Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch. The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 75 was to be borne jointly by Maersk Company and Xiamen Branch in the amount of RMB 50, and by Yinghai Company in the amount of RMB 25. The first-instance case acceptance fee was to be apportioned accordingly.

Maersk Company and its Xiamen Branch, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied to this Court for retrial, arguing: 1. Yinghai Company was merely a freight forwarding agent. Regardless of whether Maersk Company was a common carrier, the second-instance court's determination of whether Maersk Company and its Xiamen Branch's refusal to deal with Yinghai Company violated the common carrier's compulsory contracting obligation, based on legal provisions of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China and the Regulations of the People's Republic of China on International Maritime Transportation governing the relationship between shippers and carriers, constituted an error in the application of law. 2. The Container Transportation Cooperation Agreement was a freight forwarding agency agreement signed between Maersk Company's agent, Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency, and Yinghai Company. The new agreement expressly stipulated an exception: "except where the container owner or lessee explicitly indicates disagreement with entrusting the equipment to Yinghai Company for use." Maersk Company's refusal to engage in container freight forwarding business with Yinghai Company did not violate this agreement, and Maersk Company did not breach its obligations to Yinghai Company. 3. Autonomy in business operations is a kind of business qualification, which cannot be infringed upon by Maersk Company's refusal to deal with Yinghai Company. The enterprise's autonomy in business operations refers to the right of an enterprise to autonomously control, decide, and use its personnel, finances, and property internally, and the infringing party cannot be another enterprise. 4. Maersk Company does not possess the characteristics of a common carrier, such as public welfare nature, monopoly, and regulated pricing. It does not fall under the common carrier defined in Article 289 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China and does not bear the compulsory contracting obligation towards cargo owners or freight forwarding agents. Maersk Company's refusal to deal was not illegal and did not constitute a tort. 5. Even if Maersk Company were a common carrier and Yinghai Company directly requested to contract as a shipper and was refused, Maersk Company should only bear pre-contractual liability or liability for breach of contract, not tort liability leading to a judgment for removal of nuisance or compulsory transaction. Yinghai Company did not request Maersk Company to bear pre-contractual liability. They requested the revocation of the second-instance judgment and a change of judgment to dismiss Yinghai Company's claims.

Yinghai Company argued in reply: 1. Maersk Company and its Xiamen Branch's refusal to deal violated the maritime cargo transportation contract between them and Yinghai Company. The Container Transportation Cooperation Agreement was an agreement signed by Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency, representing carrier Maersk Company, with Yinghai Company during the performance of the maritime cargo transportation contract regarding the use of containers. This agreement is an integral part of the maritime cargo transportation contract. According to common practice in the maritime market, only after the parties have signed a maritime cargo transportation contract does the issue of collecting empty containers and their seals arise. Collecting empty containers and their seals is a step in performing the contract after its formation. Yinghai Company's request to collect empty containers and their seals indicates that both parties had already begun performing the maritime cargo transportation contract, which sufficiently proves that the maritime cargo transportation contract had been concluded earlier. There was no need for Yinghai Company to provide evidence of the maritime cargo transportation contract. Yinghai Company is a person who contracts with the carrier in the name of a shipper, falling under the category of contracting shipper as defined in Article 42, Item (3), Sub-item 1 of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China. Given the existence of the transportation contract, Maersk Company's refusal to allow Yinghai Company to collect containers and their seals violated the contract's terms. 2. Maersk Company and its Xiamen Branch's refusal to deal violated legal provisions. Liner shipping has characteristics of public transportation, such as public welfare nature, monopoly, and regulated pricing. Maersk Company operates liner shipping and is a common carrier. Its refusal to deal violated Article 289 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China regarding the compulsory contracting obligation of common carriers, and also violated Article 27, Item (3) of the Regulations of the People's Republic of China on International Maritime Transportation, which prohibits operators of international ship transportation services from abusing their advantageous position to cause harm to the other party through discriminatory pricing or other restrictive conditions, as well as the provisions of the United Nations Convention on a Code of Conduct for Liner Conferences, which stipulate that conference practices shall not discriminate against shipowners, shippers, or foreign trade of any country. Maersk Company and its Xiamen Branch's refusal to allow Yinghai Company to collect containers and their seals infringed upon Yinghai Company's property rights and business operation rights, constituting a concurrent liability for breach of contract and tort. They requested the dismissal of Maersk Company and its Xiamen Branch's retrial petition.

The first-instance third party, Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency, argued: As Maersk Company's agent, Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency stopped handling business between Yinghai Company and Maersk Company based on the instruction of its principal, Maersk Company. The consequences of Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency's actions should be borne by the principal, and Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency should bear no legal liability. They requested the preservation of the second-instance court's judgment holding Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency not liable.

This Court, upon trial, finds that the facts ascertained by the first-instance court are supported by relevant evidence. None of the parties raised objections. No new evidence was submitted during this Court's retrial. This Court confirms the facts ascertained by the first-instance court.

This Court holds: This case is a dispute over damages for infringement of the right to operate an international maritime freight forwarding agency. Considering the arguments of Maersk Company, its Xiamen Branch, and Yinghai Company, the focus of the dispute is whether Maersk Company's refusal to provide containers and their seals to Yinghai Company violated the contract and legal provisions.

Yinghai Company and Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency signed the Container Transportation Cooperation Agreement twice, on October 31, 2003, and March 15, 2005, respectively. The agreement signed on October 31, 2003, was automatically extended for one year to December 31, 2004, as neither party objected. The new agreement signed on March 15, 2005, stipulated that Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency would, in principle, permit Yinghai Company to collect containers, but with a special clause: "except where the container owner or lessee explicitly indicates disagreement with entrusting the equipment to Yinghai Company for use." This means both parties agreed that if the container owner did not agree to entrust the containers to Yinghai Company for use, Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency could refuse to provide containers to Yinghai Company. Pursuant to Article 402 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, a contract concluded by an agent in its own name within the scope of authority granted by the principal, where the third party knew at the time of contracting of the agency relationship between the agent and the principal, directly binds the principal and the third party. Yinghai Company knew that Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency signed the two agreements as Maersk Company's container agent, so the two agreements directly bind Yinghai Company and Maersk Company. When Maersk Company notified Xiamen Ocean Shipping Agency on March 3, 2005, to stop providing containers and their seals to Yinghai Company, Maersk Company and Yinghai Company were no longer bound by the original agreement. Effective March 15, 2005, according to the new agreement, Maersk Company could refuse to provide containers to Yinghai Company. The liner sailing schedule announcement is a commercial advertisement through which a liner company publicizes information such as routes, voyages, vessel names, schedules, and ports of call, and constitutes an invitation to offer. In ordinary container shipping business, after a carrier accepts a shipper's or its freight forwarder's booking offer, a maritime cargo transportation contract relationship is established between the carrier and shipper. Subsequently, the carrier permits the shipper to collect empty containers from the carrier or its container agent for loading, meaning both parties begin to perform the contract for transporting specific containers of cargo. The carrier's permission for the shipper to collect containers, as an act of performing the transportation contract, can confirm that the parties have concluded a transportation contract. However, the carrier's refusal to allow the shipper to collect containers does not indicate that both parties have begun performing the transportation contract, nor can it prove that a transportation contract relationship was previously established. The party claiming the existence of a transportation contract relationship bears the burden of proof for the fact of contract formation. From March 3, 2005, Maersk Company refused to allow Yinghai Company to collect containers. There was no mutual agreement on transporting containers between the parties, nor any actual transportation. Yinghai Company's claim that a maritime cargo transportation contract relationship still existed between it and Maersk Company from March 3, 2005, and that it did not need to provide proof, lacks factual and legal basis and is not supported by this Court. Maersk Company's refusal to provide containers and their seals to Yinghai Company did not violate the contract between the parties, and it does not bear liability for breach of contract.

Article 289 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China provides: "A carrier engaged in public transportation shall not reject the normal, reasonable transportation requests of passengers or shippers." Public transportation refers to transportation that provides public utility services to society and holds a monopoly position. Based on the social function of public transportation in providing transportation services to the public, and its characteristics of public welfare and monopoly, Chinese laws and regulations not only impose strict market access conditions and price controls on public transportation but also impose a compulsory contracting obligation on carriers engaged in public transportation. International maritime container liner transportation is a commercial business activity serving international trade and does not constitute a public utility; it lacks the characteristic of public welfare. Currently, whether in a specific region or globally, international liner transportation is highly competitive and does not possess monopoly characteristics. Shippers or their freight forwarding agents have considerable choice in transportation services; they can choose different liner companies or different vessels for carriage, and can also choose different routes or different modes of transportation to achieve the same transportation purpose. Pursuant to Articles 16, Paragraph 1, and 20 of the Regulations of the People's Republic of China on International Maritime Transportation, operators of international ship transportation services must obtain the qualification to operate international liner transportation business in accordance with these Regulations to operate international liner services calling at Chinese ports. International liner freight rates must be filed with the competent transport authority of the State Council. Filed freight rates include both published rates and contracted rates. Accordingly, operators of international liner transportation services can negotiate freight rates with cargo owners separately from the rates stated in their tariff schedules, and can also adjust rates according to market conditions while complying with the filing system. Although operating international liner transportation must meet statutory market access conditions, international liner freight rates do not have the characteristic of being strictly regulated like public transportation prices. Therefore, the international liner transportation engaged in by Maersk Company does not fall under the public transportation defined in Article 289 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China. Yinghai Company's claim that Maersk Company bears a compulsory contracting obligation lacks legal basis and is not supported by this Court.

Pursuant to Article 4 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, parties have the right to voluntarily conclude contracts in accordance with the law, and no unit or individual may unlawfully interfere. The freedom to conclude contracts, as enjoyed by parties according to law, includes the freedom to decide whether to conclude a contract with another party, the freedom to choose the contracting party, and the freedom to determine the contract content. Maersk Company's refusal to deal with Yinghai Company falls within the freedom to conclude contracts enjoyed by Maersk Company. Regardless of whether Maersk Company had substantively abolished container seal fees, its increase of container seal fees at the Xiamen port at that time was a general increase in transportation fees to the public, not a specific restriction targeting Yinghai Company or other specific units or individuals. There is no evidence in this case indicating that Maersk Company's refusal to deal aimed to require Yinghai Company to accept its excessively high restrictive conditions. Therefore, it is insufficient to find that Maersk Company's refusal to deal with Yinghai Company constitutes an act of abusing its advantageous position to cause harm to the other party through discriminatory pricing or other restrictive conditions under Article 27, Item (3) of the Regulations of the People's Republic of China on International Maritime Transportation. The United Nations Convention on a Code of Conduct for Liner Conferences, to which China is a party, is a convention regulating the interests of liner conferences and shipping companies, among shipping company members of a conference, between conferences or their member shipping companies and shipper organizations or representatives of shippers or shippers, and between different conferences in the provision of liner shipping services. It does not directly regulate the maritime cargo transportation contract relationship between conference member shipping companies and shippers, nor does it address the rights and obligations between non-conference member shipping companies and shippers. The principle in the Convention that conference practices shall not discriminate against shipowners, shippers, or foreign trade of any country is directed at liner conferences, not at liner companies. Maersk Company is a liner company, not a liner conference. Yinghai Company's claim that Maersk Company's refusal to deal violated the provisions of the United Nations Convention on a Code of Conduct for Liner Conferences lacks factual and legal basis and is not supported by this Court.

Yinghai Company, claiming that Maersk Company and its Xiamen Branch caused it losses by not accepting its booking of cargo on behalf of the cargo owner, requested that Maersk Company and its Xiamen Branch cease interfering with its autonomy in business operations, not refuse its shipping business, and apologize and compensate for losses. This request lacks legal basis. The first-instance judgment dismissing Yinghai Company's claims was correct. The second-instance judgment, which erroneously held Maersk Company to be a common carrier, set aside the first-instance judgment and upheld Yinghai Company's claims, was improper. The application for retrial by Maersk Company and its Xiamen Branch has merit.

In summary, the second-instance judgment incorrectly applied the law and should be corrected. Pursuant to Article 4 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 186, Paragraph 1, and Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

1. The Civil Judgment (2008) Min Min Zhong Zi No. 381 of the Fujian High People's Court is set aside;

2. The Civil Judgment (2005) Xia Hai Fa Shi Chu Zi No. 48 of the Xiamen Maritime Court is affirmed.

Court acceptance fees of RMB 75 for the first instance and RMB 75 for the second instance shall be borne by Yinghai Company.

This judgment is final.
